Q: Login failed for user '<token-identified principal>' A:

I faced the same error while getting access token. I have the following setup.

  • In ADO Service connection is used

  • Service connection is connected to Azure portal app registration/service principal which has owner access on Azure portal SQL server

  • Users created with correct roles in database inside Azure Portal database.

The reason for the error was using command "Get-AzAccessToken -ResourceUrl $resourceUrl" without using "-AsSecureString" parameter in powershell.

Using -AsSecureString fixed my issue.

Q: Why does "import a" give me an XKCD page in Spyder? A:

The most likely explanation is: Spyder has an index of modules to import and, when you type "import a", "antigravity" is the closest match; so, in order popup some autocomplete information (e.g. to list the members inside the module) Spyder imports the module under the hood.

Q: Smooth colormap in matplotlib A:

I can offer a quick hack solution based on your existing structure that should probably be good enough for its intended purpose. To do any better would require computing just noticeable differences between adjacent elements across the colour LUT and ensuring that they stay below the threshold of visibility (or differ by the same amount whichever is larger).

What I did was a quick hack to some old visual basic code for 256 level CLUT spectrum palette along the lines of your python code. This is that code snippet computing r,g,b as globals from your wavelength.

Sub wav2RGB(w)
 r = 0
 g = 0
 b = 0
 If 380 <= w And w < 440 Then
   r = (440 - w) / (440 - 380)
   b = 1
 Else
   If w < 505 Then
      g = (w - 440) / (505 - 440)
      b = 1
   Else
      If w < 540 Then
        g = 1
        b = (540 - w) / (540 - 505)
       Else
          If w < 585 Then
             r = (w - 540) / (585 - 540)
             g = 1
          Else
             If w <= 675 Then
               r = 1
               g = (675 - w) / (675 - 585)
             Else
               If w < 780 Then r = 1
             End If
          End If
       End If
    End If
 End If
  factor = 1
  lum = 0.55 * g + 0.29 * r + 0.11 * b
  If (lum > 0.65 And b > 0.6) Then factor = 0.65 / lum '' fixup cyan luminance excess
  If (lum > 0.8 And r > 0.7) Then factor = 0.8 / lum   '' fixup yellow luminance excess
  
  If 380 <= w And w <= 420 Then
    factor = 0.3 + 0.7 * (w - 380) / (420 - 380) 
  Else
    If 701 <= w And w <= 780 Then
      factor = 0.3 + 0.7 * (780 - w) / (780 - 700) 
    End If
  End If
r = 255 * r * factor
g = 255 * g * factor
b = 255 * b * factor
End Sub

I have done two things to improve the situation - shifted the breakpoints and added a crude luminance correction to the two most tricky regions G+B=cyan and G+R=yellow to tame them.

Description UV Blue Cyan Green Yellow Red IR
Original 380 440 490 510 580 645 780
Modified 380 440 505 540 585 675 780

The two most important changes are blue-cyan was 20 is now 35 and yellow-red was 65 now 90. Combined with the luminance trick this gets them below perceptual thresholds (at least for me). This is the resulting sample spectrum in Excel.

Your code might benefit from handling the break points systematically and defining behaviour for all wavelengths shorter than each each of the various thresholds in the elif sequence. You then only need a single test for wavelength shorter than next threshold and can do away with the truncs. Once the gradients are parameterised you only have to alter the single array values to move the transitions around. There are too many identical numeric constants as it is presently coded.
